facts.fact_text: The case concerns the dispersal by the police of a demonstration organised by a political party.
At the time of the events giving rise to the present application, the applicants were members of the Turkish Grand National Assembly.
The police warned the participants several times that the demonstration on 3 June 2010 was unlawful and ordered them to disperse immediately.
The police warned the participants that if they failed to disperse, the police would use force.
According to police reports, at about 4.40 p.m. on 3 June 2010, the applicants joined the front lines of demonstrators.
Shortly after the applicants joined the front lines, the group of demonstrators, accompanied by the BDP bus, began marching on the main road towards the police.
As the demonstrators continued to march despite another warning, the police dispersed them by using water cannon and tear gas.
During the first moments of the police intervention on 3 June 2010, the second applicant fell to the ground and sustained injuries to her hip.

At the material time, section 10 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) required that in order for a meeting to take place, the governor's office or authorities of the district in which the demonstration is planned must be informed, during opening hours and at least seventy-two hours prior to the meeting, by a notice containing the signature of all the members of the organising committee.
Section 22 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911), as in force at the material time, prohibited demonstrations and processions on public streets and highways.

Section 24 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law no. 2911) provided that demonstrations and processions which did not comply with the provisions of the Act would be dispersed by force on the order of the governor's office and after the demonstrators had been warned.

Under section 16 of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police, when faced with resistance in the performance of their duties, the police may use force for the purpose of, and to the extent necessary for, breaking down such resistance.

Under section 16 of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police, the use of force means recourse to physical and material force and weaponry in order to immobilise those resisting the police, in a graduated manner depending on the nature and degree of resistance.
Under section 16 of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police, the term 'material force' is defined as including handcuffs, truncheons, pressurised water and tear gas.

Under section 16 of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police, a warning is required before using force; however, depending on the nature and degree of resistance, it may also be possible to use force without any warning.

Under section 16 of Law no. 2559 on the Duties and Powers of the Police, the police determine the equipment and the degree of force to be used, and where the action is taken against a group, that determination is made by the supervisor of the intervening unit.

On 29 May 2010 the security forces received an intelligence report indicating that as of 1 June 2010 the PKK (Workers' Party of Kurdistan) would incite people to acts of civil disobedience across the country.
The intelligence report received on 29 May 2010 mentioned possible attacks against the security forces involving the use of stones, sticks and Molotov cocktails as well as the burning of vehicles.
The intelligence report received on 29 May 2010 mentioned possible attacks against public buildings involving the use of stones, sticks and Molotov cocktails as well as the burning of vehicles.
The police report of 2 June 2010 mentioned that the group might, if provoked, attack the security forces and their vehicles with stones.

On 3 June 2010 the Silopi Security Directorate issued an internal document outlining the measures to be taken and the instructions to be followed by the police before and during the forthcoming demonstration.

The internal document issued by the Silopi Security Directorate on 3 June 2010 instructed that police officers were to avoid provoking the demonstrators, follow the warning procedure at all times and comply with the chain of command.

The internal document issued by the Silopi Security Directorate on 3 June 2010 instructed that force might be used in a graduated manner only if necessary and subject to the instructions of the superior officer.
The chief inspectors' report mentioned that the police had warned the protestors many times that the demonstration was unlawful and had ordered them to disperse.

The chief inspectors' report stated that as the crowd had not stopped advancing towards the police, the police had used water cannon and tear gas, prompted by concerns that it would become impossible to intervene if the crowd reached the police barricade.
The chief inspectors' report mentioned that the police had warned the protestors many times that the demonstration was unlawful and had ordered them to disperse.

The chief inspectors' report stated that as the crowd had not stopped advancing towards the police, the police had used water cannon and tear gas, prompted by concerns that it would become impossible to intervene if the crowd reached the police barricade.
The chief inspectors' report stated that the police intervention had lasted eight to ten seconds and that pressurised water had been sprayed only once.

The chief inspectors' report stated that there was nothing to indicate that the members of parliament had been targeted by the police officers, and that it was pure coincidence that the second applicant had been hit by water (tamamen tesadüfen suya hedef olduğu).
The chief inspectors' report stated that the injury sustained by the second applicant had been the result of her falling awkwardly (biçimsiz bir şekilde) owing to physical weakness.
The chief inspectors' report noted that the other demonstrators who had been hit by the same pressurised water had not been injured.

The chief inspectors' report found that the police had intervened at the right moment, given that there had been more than three thousand demonstrators and that their number could have reached ten thousand at any moment.
The chief inspectors' report found that there had been no serious injuries apart from that of the second applicant.
The video footage shows that pressurised water was sprayed more than once during the police intervention on 3 June 2010.
The video footage shows that the traffic on the road in question was not stopped until the demonstrators began heading towards the BDP bus.
The video footage shows that the police intervention began less than two minutes after the applicants joined the front lines of demonstrators.
The video footage shows that some of the demonstrators reacted against the stone-throwing behaviour of the adolescents.
The video footage shows that the vast majority of the participants were not involved in any violent act during the period before the intervention of the police.
The video footage shows some demonstrators throwing stones at the police after the dispersal of the march.
On an unknown date the Silopi public prosecutor's office initiated, of its own motion, an investigation into the events of 3 June 2010.

On 8 June 2010 the Silopi public prosecutor's office requested information from the District Governor's Office of Silopi as to whether a preliminary investigation into the events of 3 June 2010 had been initiated pursuant to Law no. 4483.

On 8 June 2010 the Silopi public prosecutor's office requested that a decision be taken on whether to authorise the prosecution of the law-enforcement personnel in Silopi for the offence of misconduct in office.
On 28 June 2010 the applicants filed a complaint against the police officers and other officials involved in the incidents of 3 June 2010.
In their complaint of 28 June 2010, the applicants claimed that they had been ill-treated.
In their complaint of 28 June 2010, the applicants claimed that their right to freedom of expression had been violated.
In their complaint of 28 June 2010, the applicants claimed that their right to freedom of assembly had been violated.

On 9 February 2012 the Silopi public prosecutor issued a decision not to bring a prosecution against the law-enforcement personnel and their superior officers in relation to the events of 3 June 2010.

The Silopi public prosecutor, referring to the Ministry of the Interior's decision of 30 December 2010, considered that no prosecution could be brought in respect of the offence of misconduct in office, since the latter fell within the scope of Law no. 4483 on the prosecution of civil servants.

The Silopi public prosecutor reiterated the conclusions of the chief inspectors' report of 14 September 2010 and found that there was no indication that the officials had acted with an intention to directly or indirectly inflict bodily harm.
The Silopi public prosecutor found that no negligence was attributable to the law-enforcement personnel and their superior officers in relation to the events of 3 June 2010.

The Silopi public prosecutor held that freedom of expression and of assembly were subject to limitations and that the intervention of the security forces in an unlawful demonstration could not be regarded as preventing the exercise of the right to freedom of expression or other rights of the applicants.
On 21 March 2012 the applicants objected to the Silopi public prosecutor's decision of 9 February 2012 not to bring a prosecution.
The Silopi public prosecutor's decision of 9 February 2012 was amenable to judicial review except in so far as it concerned the alleged offence of misconduct in office.
On 8 May 2012 the Siirt Assize Court dismissed the applicants' objection to the Silopi public prosecutor's decision of 9 February 2012.
The Siirt Assize Court dismissed the applicants' objection on the grounds that the demonstration had not been duly notified to the authorities.
The Siirt Assize Court dismissed the applicants' objection on the grounds that the demonstrators had been warned and ordered to disperse.
The Siirt Assize Court dismissed the applicants' objection on the grounds that the injuries complained of had occurred in a moment of panic during the police intervention.
The Siirt Assize Court dismissed the applicants' objection on the grounds that there had been no direct intervention by the police officers against the applicants.
The Government provided the Court with several video recordings made by the police during the events of 3 June 2010.
The video footage shows the second applicant in the front lines of demonstrators immediately before the spraying of pressurised water towards that area.
Although it is impossible to see clearly the exact moment when the second applicant fell, the video footage shows that she was on the ground immediately after the first round of water spraying.
The video footage shows that pressurised water was sprayed more than once during the police intervention on 3 June 2010.

Human Rights Council Resolution 38/11 calls upon States to investigate any death or significant injury, including those that lead to disability, incurred during protests, including those resulting from the discharge of firearms or the use of less-lethal weapons by officials exercising law enforcement duties or by private personnel acting on behalf of the State.

Human Rights Council Resolution 38/11 encourages States to make appropriate protective equipment and less-lethal weapons available to their officials exercising law enforcement duties in order to decrease their need to use weapons of any kind, while pursuing efforts to regulate and establish protocols for the training and use of less-lethal weapons, bearing in mind that even less-lethal weapons can result in a risk to life.

Human Rights Council Resolution 38/11 underlines the importance of thorough and independent testing of less-lethal weapons prior to procurement and deployment to establish their lethality and the extent of likely injury, and of monitoring appropriate training and use of such weapons.
The United Nations Human Rights Guidance on Less-Lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement was issued on 1 June 2020 by the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights.

The United Nations Human Rights Guidance on Less-Lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement (paragraph 7.7.2) provides that in general, water cannon should only be used in situations of serious public disorder where there is a significant likelihood of loss of life, serious injury or the widespread destruction of property.

The United Nations Human Rights Guidance on Less-Lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement (paragraph 7.7.2) provides that the deployment of water cannon should be carefully planned and managed with rigorous command and control at a senior level in order to meet the requirements of necessity and proportionality.

The United Nations Human Rights Guidance on Less-Lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement (paragraph 7.7.3) provides that water cannon should not be used against persons in elevated positions, where there is a risk of significant secondary injury.

The United Nations Human Rights Guidance on Less-Lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement (paragraph 7.7.3) identifies risks of water cannon use including hypothermia and cold-water shock in cold weather, and the risk of persons slipping or being forced by the jet against walls or other hard objects.

The United Nations Human Rights Guidance on Less-Lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement (paragraph 7.7.3) notes that certain water cannon are indiscriminate in their effects, as they are unable to target individuals accurately.

The United Nations Human Rights Guidance on Less-Lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement (paragraph 7.7.4) provides that water cannon shall not target a jet of water at an individual or group of persons at short range owing to the risk of causing permanent blindness or secondary injuries if persons are propelled energetically by the water jet.

The United Nations Human Rights Guidance on Less-Lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement (paragraph 7.7.4) provides that water cannon shall not be used against restrained persons or persons otherwise unable to move.
Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 2435 (2022) on fighting and preventing excessive and unjustified use of force by law-enforcement officers was adopted on 27 April 2022.

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 2435 (2022) calls on member States of the Council of Europe and observer States to ensure that the use of weapons and other lethal or non-lethal tools by law-enforcement agencies is thoroughly regulated by their national legislation, which should lay down instructions and safeguards against abuse.
The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights published a Human Rights Comment on 25 February 2014 entitled 'Police abuse – a serious threat to the rule of law'.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' Human Rights Comment of 25 February 2014 states that States should develop clear guidelines concerning the proportionate use of force by police, including the use of tear gas, pepper spray, water cannons and firearms in the context of demonstrations, in line with international standards.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (third edition, 2019) were prepared by the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe in consultation with the European Commission for Democracy through Law (Venice Commission) of the Council of Europe.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly (third edition, 2019), paragraph 185, provide that the use of plastic/rubber bullets, baton rounds, attenuated energy projectiles, water cannons and other forceful methods of crowd control must be strictly regulated and recorded.
